httpStatus.subtitle: Check any URL's HTTP status code, response, redirects and final destination. Find 200, 301, 302, 404 and server errors with the free LifeSeos HTTP status checker.
httpStatus.hint: Enter a complete public URL to check its HTTP response and final destination.
httpStatus.redirectYesBody: The requested URL redirected to another destination.
httpStatus.redirectNoBody: No redirect was detected for this request.
httpStatus.basicsTitle: What is an HTTP status code?
httpStatus.basicsP1: An HTTP status code is a three-digit response returned by a web server after a browser, search engine crawler or other client requests a URL.
httpStatus.basicsP2: The response indicates whether the request succeeded, redirected, failed because the resource could not be found, or encountered a server-side problem.
httpStatus.groupsBody: HTTP responses are grouped by their first digit, which makes it easier to understand how the server handled a request.
httpStatus.commonTitle: Common HTTP status codes for SEO
httpStatus.commonBody: These response codes appear frequently during technical SEO audits and website maintenance.
httpStatus.redirectP1: Redirects are normal when pages move, domains change or URL structures are updated. What matters is that redirects point users and crawlers to the correct final destination.
httpStatus.redirectP2: Checking both the requested URL and final URL can help you discover unexpected redirects and identify URLs that no longer resolve directly.
httpStatus.benefit1Body: Identify pages returning 404 or other error responses.
httpStatus.benefit2Body: Confirm whether a requested URL redirects to another destination.
httpStatus.benefit3Body: Verify the destination that users and crawlers ultimately reach.
httpStatus.benefit4Body: Detect 5xx responses that may temporarily prevent access to important pages.
httpStatus.importanceTitle: Why HTTP status codes matter for SEO
httpStatus.importanceBody: Search engines rely on HTTP responses to understand whether URLs are available, moved, missing or temporarily unavailable.
httpStatus.reason1Body: Successful HTTP responses allow crawlers to access pages and process their content.
httpStatus.reason2Body: Redirect responses indicate that users and crawlers should continue to another URL.
httpStatus.reason3Body: 4xx responses can reveal outdated links and pages that are no longer available.
httpStatus.reason4Body: 5xx errors can indicate server problems that temporarily prevent crawling and access.
httpStatus.howTitle: How to use the HTTP status checker
httpStatus.how1Body: Paste the complete webpage or website URL you want to check.
httpStatus.how2Body: Select Check status and LifeSeos will request the URL and inspect its HTTP response.
httpStatus.how3Body: Check the status code and status text to understand how the server handled the request.
httpStatus.how4Body: If the URL redirects, compare the requested URL with the final URL returned by the tool.
httpStatus.faq1Q: What is an HTTP status code?
httpStatus.faq1A: An HTTP status code is a three-digit response sent by a web server after a browser, crawler, or other client requests a URL. It indicates whether the request succeeded, redirected, failed, or encountered a server problem.
httpStatus.faq2Q: Why do HTTP status codes matter for SEO?
httpStatus.faq2A: Search engines use HTTP responses to understand whether pages are available, redirected, missing, or temporarily unavailable. Incorrect status codes can create broken links or make important pages harder to crawl correctly.
httpStatus.faq3Q: What status code should a normal webpage return?
httpStatus.faq3A: A normal accessible webpage should usually return 200 OK. If the page has permanently moved, a 301 redirect is generally more appropriate.
httpStatus.faq4Q: Is a 301 redirect bad for SEO?
httpStatus.faq4A: No. A correctly implemented 301 redirect is a standard way to indicate that a URL has permanently moved to another location.
httpStatus.faq5Q: What is the difference between 404 and 410?
httpStatus.faq5A: A 404 means the requested resource was not found, while a 410 explicitly indicates that the resource has been permanently removed.
httpStatus.shareBody: Check HTTP status codes, redirects and final URLs with this free LifeSeos technical SEO tool.

2xx.title: Successful responses
2xx.description: A 2xx status means the server successfully received and processed the request. The most common response is 200 OK.

3xx.title: Redirect responses
3xx.description: A 3xx status means the requested URL redirects to another location. Common examples include 301 permanent redirects and 302 temporary redirects.

4xx.title: Client errors
4xx.description: A 4xx status usually means the requested resource cannot be accessed. A 404 response, for example, means the page was not found.

5xx.title: Server errors
5xx.description: A 5xx response means the server encountered a problem while processing the request. These errors can prevent users and search engines from accessing a page.

200.title: OK
200.description: The page loaded successfully and is generally available to users and search engines.

301.title: Moved Permanently
301.description: The URL permanently redirects to a different location. This is commonly used when pages or domains are permanently moved.

302.title: Found / Temporary Redirect
302.description: The URL temporarily redirects elsewhere. Search engines may continue to keep the original URL in their index.

404.title: Not Found
404.description: The requested page does not exist at this URL. Broken internal links and outdated URLs frequently return this response.

410.title: Gone
410.description: The page has been intentionally and permanently removed and is not expected to return.

500.title: Internal Server Error
500.description: The server encountered an unexpected problem and could not complete the request.

503.title: Service Unavailable
503.description: The server is temporarily unavailable, often because of maintenance, overload, or another temporary issue.

pageSpeed.info3Body: Measures how long it takes for the largest visible content element in the viewport to render.
pageSpeed.info4Body: Measures visual stability by tracking unexpected movement of page elements during loading.
pageSpeed.info5Body: Measures time when long main-thread tasks can delay the browser from responding quickly.

meta.title: Robots.txt Generator — Free Crawler Rules Builder
meta.description: Generate a crawler-friendly robots.txt file for your website with the free LifeSeos robots.txt generator.

robotsTxt.subtitle: Create a free robots.txt file for your website, define crawler access rules, add your XML sitemap and generate a ready-to-use robots.txt file for search engines.
robotsTxt.userAgentHint: Use * to apply the rule group to all compatible crawlers.
robotsTxt.allowHint: Example: / allows crawling from the root unless a more specific rule restricts a path.
robotsTxt.sitemapHint: Use the full absolute URL of your XML sitemap.
robotsTxt.noteBody: Robots.txt controls crawler access. It should not be used to protect confidential or sensitive information.
robotsTxt.introP1: A robots.txt file gives supported web crawlers instructions about which areas of a website they may or may not crawl. It is normally placed at the root of the website so crawlers can discover the rules before requesting other URLs.
robotsTxt.dirUserAgentBody: Defines which crawler or group of crawlers the following rules apply to.
robotsTxt.dirAllowBody: Allows crawling of a specific path when the rule is applicable to the selected crawler.
robotsTxt.dirDisallowBody: Requests that compatible crawlers do not crawl a specified path or directory.
robotsTxt.dirSitemapBody: Provides crawlers with the absolute URL of an XML sitemap.
robotsTxt.howTitle: How to Use the Robots.txt Generator
robotsTxt.howBody: Configure the crawler rules, review the generated text and place the final file in your website root.
robotsTxt.how1Body: Use * for a general rule group or enter the crawler token you specifically want to target.
robotsTxt.how2Body: Add the paths that crawlers should be permitted or requested not to crawl.
robotsTxt.how3Body: Optionally include the full URL of your XML sitemap.
robotsTxt.how4Body: Copy the generated content and save it as robots.txt at the root of your website.
robotsTxt.distTitle: Blocking Crawling Is Not the Same as Preventing Indexing
robotsTxt.distBody: A robots.txt rule primarily controls crawling. It should not be treated as a guaranteed method for keeping a URL out of search results. If you need to control indexing, review the appropriate indexing directives and make sure search engines can access the page when those directives need to be read.
robotsTxt.tipsP1: Small robots.txt mistakes can restrict crawler access to pages or resources you intended to keep crawlable. Review every rule carefully before publishing the file.
robotsTxt.tipsP2: After making changes, verify the live robots.txt file and check that important public pages and resources are still accessible to the crawlers you want to support.
robotsTxt.tip1Body: Avoid broad Disallow rules unless you are certain the entire path should not be crawled.
robotsTxt.tip2Body: Review user-agent groups and path rules before uploading the file.
robotsTxt.tip3Body: Add your XML sitemap URL when appropriate so crawlers can discover it easily.
robotsTxt.tip4Body: Confirm that important public pages remain crawlable after updating robots.txt.
robotsTxt.mistake1Body: A broad Disallow rule can prevent crawlers from accessing far more pages than intended.
robotsTxt.mistake2Body: Restricting CSS, JavaScript or other resources can make it harder for crawlers to render a page properly.
robotsTxt.mistake3Body: Blocked paths remain publicly accessible if someone knows the URL, so sensitive data requires real access control.
robotsTxt.nextTitle: Control crawling, improve discovery and audit your site
robotsTxt.nextBody: Use these tools together to manage crawler access, provide a structured list of important URLs and then run a broader SEO audit.
robotsTxt.wf1Body: Create crawler access rules and reference your sitemap from a correctly structured robots.txt file.
robotsTxt.wf2Body: Create an XML sitemap that lists important URLs and helps search engines discover your website structure.
robotsTxt.wf3Body: Run a broader SEO audit after configuring crawling and discovery to review technical and content signals.
robotsTxt.shareBody: Create a clean robots.txt file and manage crawler access with this free LifeSeos tool.

xmlSitemap.introTitle: Help Search Engines Discover Your Pages
xmlSitemap.introP1: An XML sitemap is a file containing information about URLs you consider important on your website. Search engines can use the sitemap as an additional source for discovering and crawling those URLs.
xmlSitemap.elUrlsetBody: The main XML element that contains the URL entries in a standard XML sitemap.
xmlSitemap.elUrlBody: Groups the information associated with one webpage in the sitemap.
xmlSitemap.elLocBody: Contains the complete absolute URL of the page included in the sitemap.
xmlSitemap.elOptionalBody: Protocol fields such as changefreq and priority may be included, although individual search engines may ignore them.
xmlSitemap.howTitle: How to Use the XML Sitemap Generator
xmlSitemap.howBody: Build a sitemap from your important website URLs and make it accessible to search engines.
xmlSitemap.how1Body: Enter one complete website URL per line, including the protocol and domain.
xmlSitemap.how2Body: Select change frequency and priority values if you want them included in the XML output.
xmlSitemap.how3Body: Review the generated XML, then copy it or download the sitemap.xml file.
xmlSitemap.how4Body: Place the sitemap on your website and submit its URL through the relevant webmaster tools.
xmlSitemap.distTitle: A Sitemap Helps Discovery, but Does Not Guarantee Indexing
xmlSitemap.distBody: Submitting a sitemap helps search engines discover the URLs you want them to know about. However, inclusion in a sitemap does not guarantee that every URL will be crawled, indexed or ranked. Each page still needs to be accessible and suitable for indexing.
xmlSitemap.tipsP1: A sitemap should contain the URLs you actually want search engines to discover and potentially show in search results.
xmlSitemap.tipsP2: Use complete canonical URLs, avoid broken or redirected pages where possible and keep your sitemap updated as your website changes.
xmlSitemap.tip1Body: Include complete URLs such as https://example.com/page rather than relative paths.
xmlSitemap.tip2Body: Prefer the URL version you want search engines to treat as the primary version of the page.
xmlSitemap.tip3Body: Focus the sitemap on public pages that you actually want search engines to discover.
xmlSitemap.tip4Body: Update your sitemap when important pages are added, removed or significantly changed.
xmlSitemap.problem1Body: Sitemap entries should use complete absolute URLs rather than paths such as /about.
xmlSitemap.problem2Body: Including error pages or invalid URLs can reduce the usefulness and cleanliness of your sitemap.
xmlSitemap.problem3Body: Listing duplicate or alternate URL versions can send inconsistent signals about which URL you prefer.
xmlSitemap.nextTitle: Control crawling, improve discovery and audit your site
xmlSitemap.nextBody: Use these tools together to manage crawler access, publish a clean sitemap and then run a broader SEO audit.

keywordDensity.subtitle: Check keyword density and frequency in your content, see how often words appear and review keyword density percentages instantly.
keywordDensity.inputPlaceholder: Paste your article, landing page copy, or SEO content here...
keywordDensity.inputNote: Your text is analyzed directly in the browser as you type or paste content.
keywordDensity.empty: Paste some text to see keyword frequency and density.
keywordDensity.introTitle: Understand How Keywords Are Used in Your Content
keywordDensity.introP1: Keyword density measures how frequently a word appears compared with the total number of words in your content. It can be useful for spotting repetition, but it should be treated as a diagnostic metric rather than a target score.
keywordDensity.freqBody: Shows the number of times a specific word appears in the analyzed content.
keywordDensity.densityBody: Shows the percentage of total words represented by a particular keyword.
keywordDensity.uniqueBody: Shows how many different words appear in the text and gives context to vocabulary variety.
keywordDensity.formulaBody: The tool divides the number of times a keyword appears by the total number of words, then converts the result into a percentage.
keywordDensity.formulaExample: Example: if a word appears 5 times in 200 words, its density is 2.5%.
keywordDensity.howTitle: How to Use the Keyword Density Checker
keywordDensity.howBody: Use the report to understand which words dominate your content and whether repetition appears natural.
keywordDensity.how1Body: Add an article, landing page, product description or any other text you want to review.
keywordDensity.how2Body: Use the word counts to understand the overall size and vocabulary of the content.
keywordDensity.how3Body: See which words appear most often and how many times each one is used.
keywordDensity.how4Body: Look for unnatural repetition rather than trying to reach a fixed percentage.
keywordDensity.noteTitle: There Is No Universal “Perfect” Keyword Density
keywordDensity.noteBody: Keyword density should not be treated as a formula for rankings. A useful page should cover its topic naturally and clearly. Repeating the same phrase simply to increase a percentage can make the content less readable and less useful.
keywordDensity.avoidP1: Repeating a word or phrase more often than necessary can make writing sound unnatural. Density data is most useful when it helps you notice that kind of repetition.
keywordDensity.avoidP2: Instead of forcing exact-match keywords into every paragraph, focus on answering the topic clearly and use related terms where they make sense.
keywordDensity.practice1Body: Use keywords where they genuinely help explain the topic.
keywordDensity.practice2Body: Review unusually frequent words and decide whether repeated uses are necessary.
keywordDensity.practice3Body: Cover the subject comprehensively instead of repeating only one exact phrase.
keywordDensity.practice4Body: Make clarity, usefulness and search intent more important than a density percentage.
keywordDensity.nextTitle: Rewrite, analyze and refine your content
keywordDensity.nextBody: Use these tools together to improve your draft, review content quality and finish by checking keyword frequency and density.
keywordDensity.wf1Body: Improve clarity, tone and structure before evaluating the content in more detail.
keywordDensity.wf2Body: Review readability, structure, vocabulary and overall content quality before checking keyword repetition.
keywordDensity.wf3Body: Finish the workflow by reviewing keyword frequency, density and potentially unnatural repetition.

hashtags.title: Hashtags
hashtags.text: Use a small number of relevant hashtags rather than unrelated tags.

callToAction.title: Call to Action
callToAction.text: Give viewers one clear next step that matches the purpose of the video.

youtubeDescriptionGenerator.howTitle: How to use the YouTube Description Generator
youtubeDescriptionGenerator.howBody: Generate a structured starting point, then edit it so it matches your actual video before publishing.

1.title: Enter your video topic
1.text: Describe the main subject of the video in a clear phrase.

2.title: Add keyword and audience details
2.text: Optionally provide a keyword, target audience and call to action.

3.title: Choose a description style
3.text: Select balanced, SEO focused, professional, friendly, short or detailed.

4.title: Generate and customize
4.text: Choose a description, copy it and edit it so it accurately reflects your video.

youtubeDescriptionGenerator.whyP1: A description gives viewers additional context about the video and can help explain what they will learn, which resources are relevant and what action they can take next.
youtubeDescriptionGenerator.whyP2: The generated text should always be reviewed and customized before publishing so it accurately reflects the actual video.

explainVideo.title: Explain the video
explainVideo.text: Give viewers useful context about the topic and what the video covers.

relevance.title: Support relevance
relevance.text: Use natural topic wording that matches the actual video content.

resources.title: Add useful resources
resources.text: Include links or references only when they genuinely support the viewer.

nextAction.title: Guide the next action
nextAction.text: Use a relevant call to action without overwhelming the description.

youtubeScriptWriter.factorsTitle: Build a clearer structure before you start recording
youtubeScriptWriter.factorsBody: A useful script gives the video direction without making it sound robotic. Use the generated structure as a starting point, then adjust the wording to match your own voice.

hook.title: Strong Hook
hook.text: Give viewers a clear reason to keep watching from the beginning.

intro.title: Clear Introduction
intro.text: Set expectations and explain what the video will cover.

points.title: Main Talking Points
points.text: Break the topic into logical sections instead of one long block.

pacing.title: Better Pacing
pacing.text: Use video length to keep the number of sections realistic.

audience.title: Audience Fit
audience.text: Adapt the explanation to the people the video is designed for.

cta.title: Relevant CTA
cta.text: End with a next step that matches the purpose of the video.

youtubeScriptWriter.howTitle: How to use the YouTube Script Writer
youtubeScriptWriter.howBody: Use the tool to create a structured first draft, then rewrite sections so the final script sounds natural in your own voice.

1.title: Enter your video topic
1.text: Describe what your video is mainly about.

2.title: Choose style and length
2.text: Select the tone you want and the approximate video duration.

3.title: Add audience and goal
3.text: Optionally explain who the video is for and what you want it to achieve.

4.title: Generate and personalize
4.text: Review the script structure, copy useful sections and adapt the wording before recording.

youtubeScriptWriter.whyP1: A script can help creators organize ideas, reduce repetition and keep the video moving in a clear direction. It can also make recording easier because the main talking points are already planned.
youtubeScriptWriter.whyP2: The generated script is a starting point, not a finished performance. Review and personalize the wording so it matches your real content and speaking style.

rambling.title: Reduce rambling
rambling.text: Keep the video focused by deciding the main points before recording.

flow.title: Improve flow
flow.text: Use transitions so each part of the video connects naturally.

planning.title: Save planning time
planning.text: Start with a structured outline instead of a blank page.

voice.title: Sound more intentional
voice.text: Give each section a clear purpose while keeping your own voice.
